items.label: text
items.text: The packing in the solid might be completely different. What is important is that the particles are close together and, usually, regularly packed. When you draw a liquid, make sure the particles are mostly touching the particles next to them.

items.label: list_item
items.text: You can't walk through a brick wall because of the strong forces of attraction between the particles - the particles can't move out of your way.

items.label: list_item
items.text: You can swim through water because you can push the particles out of the way.

items.label: list_item
items.text: It is easy to move through a gas because there are no forces between the particles.

items.label: section_header
items.text: CHANGING STATE BETWEEN SOLID AND LIQUID

items.label: text
items.text: The arrangement of the particles in solids, liquids and gases explains these facts.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 1.4 The arrangement of particles in different states of matter

items.label: text
items.text: In a solid, the particles are usually arranged regularly and packed closely together. The particles are only able to vibrate about fixed positions; they can't move around. The particles have strong forces of attraction between them, which keep them together.

items.label: text
items.text: In a liquid, the particles are still mostly touching, but some gaps have appeared. This is why liquids are usually less dense than solids. The forces between the particles are less effective, and the particles can move around each other. The particles in a liquid are arranged randomly.

items.label: text
items.text: The particles in a gas are moving randomly at high speed in all directions. In a gas, the particles are much further apart and there are (almost) no forces of attraction between them.

items.label: text
items.text: The particles in a solid have less kinetic (movement) energy than the particles in a liquid, which have less kinetic energy than the particles in a gas.

items.label: section_header
items.text: INTERCONVERSIONS BETWEEN THE THREE STATES OF MATTER

items.label: text
items.text: If you heat a solid, the energy provided by the heat source makes the particles in the solid vibrate faster and faster. Eventually, they vibrate so fast that the forces of attraction between the particles are no longer strong enough to hold them together; the particles are then able to move around each other – the solid melts to form a liquid. The temperature at which the solid melts is called its melting point. The particles in the liquid have more kinetic energy than the particles in the solid so energy has to be supplied to convert a solid to a liquid.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 1.5 Melting to become a liquid – and freezing to become a solid.

items.label: text
items.text: If the liquid is cooled again, the liquid particles will move around more and more slowly. Eventually, they are moving so slowly that the forces of attraction between them will hold them in a fixed position and the particles pack more closely together into a solid. The liquid freezes, forming a solid. The temperature at which this occurs is called the freezing point.

items.label: text
items.text: Although they are called different things depending which way you are going, the temperature of the melting point and that of the freezing point of a substance are exactly the same.
